title: A phase portrait with nullclines: what are the equilibria and their stability?
summary: For a two-variable system the plane of the two variables is filled with flow lines. The nullclines (where one variable stops changing) cross at the equilibria, and the type of each equilibrium (stable spiral, saddle, ...) is read from the flow around it.

media.alt: A phase plane with grey flow lines. Teal solid lines are the x-nullcline: the vertical axis and a falling diagonal. Blue dashed lines are the y-nullcline: the horizontal axis and the vertical line x = 0.4. An amber dot at (0.4, 0.6) is a stable spiral with flow lines spiralling in; pink crosses at (0, 0) and (1, 0) are saddles.
media.caption: Reference render of class F4.7 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: What are the equilibria and their stability?
read_the_figure.axes: x: prey (horizontal, -0.05 to 1.3). y: predator (vertical, -0.05 to 1.3). Grey lines: flow lines. Teal: the x-nullcline (x' = 0). Blue dashed: the y-nullcline (y' = 0). Amber dot: stable spiral; pink crosses: saddles. The equations are printed at the top left: x' = x(1 - x - y), y' = y(x - 0.4).
look_at: Where do a teal and a blue line cross? Those are the equilibria.
Which equilibrium do the interior flow lines wind into?
At the two saddles, along which direction do lines come in and along which do they leave?
On the nullclines, in what direction does the flow cross: vertical or horizontal?
as_drawn: Equilibria: (0, 0) and (1, 0), saddles, and (0.4, 0.6), a stable spiral. The labels are typed on the figure with their coordinates.
The Jacobian eigenvalues are 1 and -0.4 at (0, 0), -1 and 0.6 at (1, 0), and -0.2 plus or minus 0.447i at (0.4, 0.6).
Flow lines are thin, grey and sparse in the upper right, so the exit from the window is not shown; the legend sits over part of the field.
read_the_figure.proves: That the plotted equilibria are where the nullclines meet, and what type each is according to the labelled linear analysis. It does not prove there are no other equilibria outside the window.
if_wrong: Equilibria not typed: 'the dots' have no meaning.
Nullclines missing: the reader cannot find the equilibria from the picture.
Flow lines drawn so sparsely that a spiral looks like a node.

terms.meaning: The set of trajectories of a system in the plane of its variables, time not shown.
A point where all rates of change vanish.
A curve where one variable's rate is zero: the flow there is vertical (for x) or horizontal (for y).
An equilibrium that trajectories spiral into: eigenvalues complex with negative real part.
An equilibrium that attracts along one direction and repels along another: one positive and one negative eigenvalue.
The matrix of partial derivatives of the right-hand sides at the equilibrium; its eigenvalues give the local behaviour.

remember: Equilibria = intersections of an x-nullcline with a y-nullcline.
tr J < 0 and det J > 0: stable; det J < 0: saddle; tr^2 < 4 det: spiral.
On the x-nullcline flow is vertical; on the y-nullcline it is horizontal.
Type every fixed point; show nullclines.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position is the state (x, y). Grey lines show where trajectories go, with arrowheads for direction. Teal and blue lines are the nullclines (colour and dash tell them apart); amber dots and pink crosses are the typed equilibria. Text gives the equations.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Time disappears: a trajectory is a curve in the plane, and the whole family of curves is a map of all possible behaviours. The nullclines organise it: they cut the plane into regions where the flow has fixed directions (up and right, up and left, etc.), and equilibria sit where they cross. Linear analysis types each equilibrium, and the picture confirms it.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Only the window is shown: trajectories leave it, equilibria may lie outside. Sparse flow lines can make a spiral look like a node. Linearisation can fail: a centre (eigenvalues purely imaginary) is not decided by the linear terms. And a picture without time hides how fast: a trajectory that crawls near a saddle looks the same as one that rushes past.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Typed fixed points turn dots into statements. Nullclines make the equilibria findable without computation and explain why the flow arrows turn where they do. Both are the checklist; together they turn a pretty picture into an analysis.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A time-series plot for chosen initial conditions shows how fast. A table of eigenvalues types each equilibrium exactly. A basin-of-attraction map colours the plane by the equilibrium reached. A bifurcation diagram shows how equilibria change with a parameter, here the value 0.4.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour the plane by the sign pattern of (x', y') and print the Jacobian eigenvalues next to each equilibrium; add three time-series insets for starting points (0.1, 0.1), (1, 1), (0.9, 0.05).

steps.title: Find the equilibria
steps.note: The x-nullclines are x = 0 and x + y = 1; the y-nullclines are y = 0 and x = 0.4. Their crossings are the three equilibria; x = 0 and x = 0.4 never meet.

steps.title: Type them with the Jacobian
steps.note: (0, 0): det -0.4 < 0, saddle. (1, 0): det -0.6 < 0, saddle. (0.4, 0.6): trace -0.4, det 0.24, tr^2 = 0.16 < 4 det = 0.96: eigenvalues -0.2 plus or minus 0.447i, a stable spiral. A simulation from (1, 1) ends at (0.4, 0.6).

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) list the equilibria and how you found them. (2) Which one attracts the interior? (3) What happens along the vertical axis x = 0?

solution.text: Where a teal line crosses a blue dashed one: (0, 0), (1, 0) and (0.4, 0.6).
The amber dot at (0.4, 0.6): the flow lines spiral inward, eigenvalues -0.2 plus or minus 0.447i.
On x = 0 the first equation gives x' = 0, and y' = -0.4 y: the flow is straight down toward the origin, the stable direction of the saddle at (0, 0).

worked.answer: Three equilibria: two saddles and a stable spiral at (0.4, 0.6); interior trajectories end there; the vertical axis is the stable direction of the origin saddle.

analyze.q: Why can't the nullclines x = 0 and x = 0.4 produce an equilibrium?
A system has eigenvalues plus and minus i at an equilibrium. Why is the picture inconclusive?
How would the portrait change if the 0.4 were raised to 1.2?

evaluate.q: A reviewer says 'the spiral may really be a node at this resolution'. What data would settle it?
evaluate.hint: The sign of the discriminant tr^2 - 4 det.

create: Add the regions of constant sign (x' > 0 or < 0, y' > 0 or < 0) as four shades.
Plot x(t) and y(t) from (1, 1) and read the decay rate and the oscillation period.

checks.q: Where are equilibria found on a nullcline plot?
checks.answer: At the crossings of an x-nullcline with a y-nullcline.

checks.q: A Jacobian has trace -0.4 and determinant 0.24. What kind of equilibrium is it?
checks.answer: Stable (trace negative, determinant positive); tr^2 = 0.16 < 4 det = 0.96, so a spiral.

checks.q: A fixed point has eigenvalues 1 and -0.4. Describe how trajectories behave nearby.
checks.answer: A saddle: approach along the stable direction (eigenvalue -0.4), leave along the unstable direction (eigenvalue 1); generic paths pass by and turn away.
